<STRUCT_0001>
It follows from the lemmas in Sections <REF_0001> and
<REF_0002> that any open (resp.<SPACE_0001>closed) immersion of
schemes is isomorphic to the inclusion of an open (resp.<SPACE_0002>closed) subscheme
of the target.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
Our definition of a closed immersion is halfway between Hartshorne
and EGA. Hartshorne defines a closed immersion as a morphism <MATH_0001> of
schemes which induces a homeomorphism of <MATH_0002> onto a closed subset of
<MATH_0003> such that <MATH_0004> is surjective, see
<REF_0003>. We will show this is equivalent to our notion in
Lemma <REF_0004>. In <REF_0005>,
Grothendieck and Dieudonn<ACCENT_0001> first define closed subschemes
via the construction of Example <REF_0006>
using quasi-coherent sheaves of ideals and then define a closed immersion
as a morphism <MATH_0005> which induces an isomorphism with a
closed subscheme. It follows from Lemma <REF_0007>
that this agrees with our notion.

<STRUCT_0004><STRUCT_0005>
Pedagogically speaking the definition above is a disaster/nightmare.
In teaching this material to students, we have found it often
convenient to define a closed immersion as an affine morphism
<MATH_0006> of schemes such that <MATH_0007>
is surjective. Namely, it turns out that the notion of an affine
morphism (Morphisms, Section <REF_0008>)
is quite natural and easy to understand.

<STRUCT_0006><STRUCT_0007>
For more information on closed immersions we suggest the reader visit
Morphisms, Sections <REF_0009> and
<REF_0010>.

<STRUCT_0008><STRUCT_0009>
We will discuss locally closed subschemes and immersions
at the end of this section.
